It also implies that attention should be paid to the accuracy of the aerodynamic modeling. Our model does not include the impact of car ordering. For example, mixing different cars with different profiles can have a significant impact on aerodynamic drag. It is difficult to separate rolling and curve drag from gradient drag, but the gradient power is also shown as recoverable as a power source. 10 Fig. 8 Detailed view of all power flows for optimal powering policy. The optimal powering policy results in reduced energy consumption and can result is shorter travel times. The naïve policy starts with maximum power and tries to follow the maximum speeds as indicated in the study. For hybrid power situations this will often result in the battery state of charge depleting before the end of the route, resulting in lower available power and may result in longer overall travel times. The optimal powering policy does require some initial iterating to determine the maximum feasible travel speed that is less than or equal to the user supplied maximum travel speed. The distance-based integration makes the computational burden reasonable. Once a feasible travel speed is determined, the optimization can complete without difficulties. The improvement in fuel and time using the optimal powering policy is made possible because we can look ahead to all of the power and energy requirements throughout the route. The robustness of this solution is currently not investigated. The real world operation of consists on routes includes in scheduled stops for random periods of time. These stops are caused by meets and passes where one consist pulls over to an auxiliary track to wait for another consists to pass. This results in increased energy consumed for braking, idling, and accelerating. It also increases the overall travel time for the route. There may be more robust solutions that use a limited look ahead strategy that should be investigated. These may include a more detailed heuristic strategy than the current naïve policy or a more complicated dynamic programming or model predictive controller (MPC). VI. Conclusions We have provided the details to the algorithms used in the SCORE toolset. This is an open-source set of tools that are made freely available as source code from GitHub and as a running web application hosted on Amazon Web Services. The details for the implement of these algorithms can be found in the source code located on GitHub. We anticipate this as a starting point for conversations with industry and the government on developing new energy technologies and policies to improve both greenhouse gas emissions and reduced operating expenses.
